title: Compress a Bit Grid Into Quadrants
statement:
You get an n × n grid of 0s and 1s, where n is a power of two. Compress it into a quadtree:

  • If every cell of the current square has the same value, the square becomes a leaf: just that value, 0 or 1.
  • Otherwise split it into four equal squares and compress each one. The square becomes a list of the four results in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right.

Return the compressed form of the whole grid. Instead of node objects, a leaf is a number and an inner node is a 4-element list, so the result is a nested list such as [1, 0, 0, [0, 1, 1, 1]].

examples.why: The whole grid is one value, so it is a single leaf.
Mixed, so split into four 1×1 squares: top-left 1, top-right 0, bottom-left 0, bottom-right 0.
Three 2×2 quadrants are uniform and become leaves. Only the bottom-right one is mixed and splits again.

hints: Write a function that compresses the square with top-left corner (top, left) and side size. When is it a leaf?
Recurse on the four quarters first. If all four results are leaves with the same value, the whole square is uniform, so return that value instead of a list.
Building bottom-up this way reads every cell exactly once, at the 1×1 level, so the whole job is O(n²) with no separate uniformity scan.

explain.intuition:
This is divide and conquer on a square. A square is either uniform, which makes it a leaf, or it is four smaller squares, each compressed the same way. The direct version scans the square to test uniformity and then recurses. That rescans each cell once per level, O(n² log n).

Turning it around avoids the rescans: compress the four quarters first, then look at their results. The square is uniform exactly when all four children came back as the same leaf. A 1×1 square is always a leaf. Every cell is read once, at the bottom. It is like collapsing identical nested DOM wrappers: you only know a wrapper is redundant after you have simplified its children.
steps: Let h = size / 2 and build the four quarters: (top, left), (top, left + h), (top + h, left), (top + h, left + h).
If all four are numbers and equal, return that number.
Otherwise return the list of the four results. The answer is build(0, 0, n).
pitfalls: Mixing up the quadrant order. It is top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right: row offset first, then column offset.
Merging four children that are all lists of the same shape. Only four equal leaves merge.
Swapping row and column when splitting, which mirrors the tree along the diagonal.

complexity.space: O(n²) for the output, O(log n) recursion

solutions.title: Scan for uniformity, then split
solutions.idea: Check whether the square has one value by scanning it. If yes, return a leaf; otherwise recurse on four quarters.

solutions.title: Build the quarters first, merge equal leaves
solutions.idea: Compress the four quarters, then collapse them into one leaf when all four are the same leaf. Each cell is read once.

followups: Given two compressed grids, compute the compressed form of their cell-wise OR without expanding them.
The grid is not square or its side is not a power of two. How would you pad or adapt the split?
